nodes.name: Every prime natural number is odd
nodes.content: For every natural number p, if p is prime, then p is odd.

nodes.name: Euclid's lemma for natural numbers
nodes.content: For natural numbers p, m, n: if p is prime and p divides m·n, then p divides m or p divides n.

sources.edition: Thomas L. Heath English translation; Perseus Book VII
sources.inspection: Web text inspected. Proposition states that if a prime measures a product of two numbers, it measures one of the original numbers.

sources.edition: Online presentation of Euclid, Elements, Book IX, Proposition 20
sources.inspection: Web text independently re-opened as a second presentation. The same proof skeleton and explicit VII.31 dependency are visible. This is a cross-source consistency check, not independent mathematical review.
Documentation exposes the exceptional prime 2 in parity theorems and the product-divisibility theorem for primes.

observed_structure: Begin with an assigned finite multitude of primes.
Form a number measured by the assigned primes and add one.
Split on whether the resulting number is prime or composite.
In the composite case invoke Book VII Proposition 31 to obtain a prime divisor.
Show that divisor is not one of the assigned primes because otherwise it would divide the difference, one.
cross_source_checks.caveat: Both presentations are closely related modern presentations of Euclid and do not constitute independent mathematical review.

assumptions_or_framework: natural-number divisibility in Euclid Book VII terminology
proofs.method: Assume the prime does not divide one factor; Euclid VII.29 gives coprimality, and preceding ratio/divisibility results are used to conclude divisibility of the other factor.

formalizations.formal_expression_summary: Nat.Prime.dvd_mul {p m n : ℕ} (pp : Prime p) : p ∣ m * n ↔ p ∣ m ∨ p ∣ n

counterexamples.scope: Natural numbers under the modern Mathlib-style prime/parity context
counterexamples.explanation: The source documentation includes Nat.prime_two, and for a prime p gives Even p ↔ p = 2. Therefore 2 is a prime even natural number and witnesses failure of the universal claim that every prime is odd.

witness_support.note: Mathlib documentation records a theorem that 2 is prime; this project has not locally recompiled it.
For a prime p, Mathlib documents Even p ↔ p = 2. Instantiating at p=2 together with Nat.prime_two yields the even witness used here; independent formal replay is pending.
